newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar eases vs yen and mark by late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dollar eases vs yen and mark by late Tokyo.

text.p: The dollar had eased against the yen and the mark by late-afternoon Tokyo on Tuesday after earlier hitting a new 37-month high against the mark, partly on mark weakness against the yen in cross trade.
But afternoon trade was thin due to a lack of fresh factors in Japan, while the dollar's topside remained heavy amid lingering concern over possible Bank of Japan intervention.
The dollar hit 1.7350 marks, its highest level since February 1994 in the morning, as traders sold the German currency for yen to trigger stop-loss selling at 73.00 yen.

Additional sales of marks for yen were detected in the afternoon, aimed at setting off more stop-loss selling around 72.80 yen. Those sales indirectly pushed the dollar down below 126.20 yen, an initial support point, dealers said.
Later in the afternoon, the dollar eased against the mark on possible profit-taking, dipping as low as 1.7282 marks. Dollar/yen rates were dragged down in tandem.
"Trade was directionless," a city bank dealer said, adding that no major factor was detected for dollar sales for marks in the afternoon.
Dealers said traders were reluctant to test the dollar's topside during the Asian session as they remained cautious over possible dollar-selling intervention.

The city bank dealer said it was not easy to buy dollars aggressively for yen for the same reason, although that might not be the case in dollar/mark trade because European monetary authorities seemed less nervous than Japanese authorities about the dollar's recent rise against their currencies.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Monday, when asked about possible U.S.-Japan joint intervention to prop up the yen, that U.S. policy was unchanged. He added: "We'll act when it's appropriate and not act when it's not appropriate."
His comment had little impact in Tokyo, but some said they took it to mean that a joint intervention was unlikely.
"I think the United States will not conduct concerted intervention until a Group of Seven meeting (later this month)," a trust bank dealer said.
The market is now focusing on the release of U.S. consumer price index (CPI) data for March due at 1230 GMT.
Economists polled by Reuters expected the CPI to rise 0.2 percent. Excluding food and energy items, the CPI is seen up 0.3 percent.
Some said although the Dow Industrials rallied strongly on Monday, closing unofficially at 6,452, they remained a little nervous about how the CPI data would affect U.S. asset markets.

Dealers said overall dollar/yen trade was thin and trapped in a narrow range, with support expected near 126.00 yen amid steady investors' bids, and offers detected around 126.60 yen. -- Yoko Nishikawa in Tokyo +81-3-3432-8584
